opening.headline: Find out who manages sessions and state so that conversations can continue even when the server restarts.
body: Let's say the server restarts while a user is placing an order over several turns. Even if the same user says, "Go ahead with what I said earlier," the agent doesn't know what they mean. This is because the conversation history and progress were only in the memory of the server process.

In this class, we explain the concepts of session, state, and event, and compare the way ADK, OpenAI Agents SDK, and Claude Agent SDK continue conversations in the same framework. We also distinguish between when the state is managed by the app and when the platform manages it, and use examples to explain what happens when the range of the state key is set incorrectly.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the concepts of sessions, states, and events
You can distinguish between when the state is managed by the app and when the state is managed by the platform.

screens.title: Conversations disappear when server restarts
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the same request behaves before and after the server is restarted.

visual.alt: A scene where there is a conversation only within the server process and then disappears upon restart.
labels: Please proceed with what I said earlier.

states.label: Before restart
states.body: A user is placing an order over several turns. I chose the menu on the first turn, decided on the quantity on the second turn, and entered the delivery address on the third turn. The agent knows all of this flow, so he naturally follows up with the next question. This is because the conversation history and progress are in the memory of the server process.

states.label: After restart
states.body: After the server restarts, the same user requests "Proceed with what I said earlier." The agent doesn't know what was said earlier, so he asks the question again from the beginning or gives a wrong answer. Since the conversation history and progress were only in process memory, they disappeared with the process. From the user's perspective, they have to repeat from the beginning what they have already done.

screens.outro: There is one key question in this lesson: Who records and where does the conversation come back?

screens.title: Think about it: a broken conversation
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever seen an app suddenly restart and your conversations are reset?
items.answer: Because of deployment, failover, and autoscaling, server processes restart more often than you might think. If the conversation history is only in process memory, all users will be disconnected each time. So the conversation must be recorded outside the process.

items.prompt: Think of a situation where you had to carry a conversation across multiple devices or processes.
items.answer: If you have multiple servers, the next request from the same user may go to a different server. At this time, you must be able to find and load the conversation using its identifier to continue it on any server.

items.prompt: Look back and see where you wrote down your steps.
items.answer: Progressive steps can be scattered across sentences in the conversation record, or they can be set aside as separate status values. Leaving them as state values ​​makes them easier to read and write and reduces the need for the model to interpret them. In this lesson we will look at that structure.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's start by checking out what ADK's sessions contain.

screens.title: ADK Session: The Courage of One Conversation Thread
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: ADK's Session is a container that holds one conversation thread between a user and an agent. The session is identified by id, app_name, user_id, and this session ID serves as the key to retrieve the same conversation later. Within the session, there exists events. events is an event log that records user messages, agent responses, and tool actions in chronological order. Additionally, state exists. state contains temporary data used exclusively within this conversation, along with the timestamp of the last update. The creation, retrieval, addition, and deletion of sessions are managed by SessionService. Since the agent code does not directly interact with the storage but instead goes through the service, the agent code can remain unchanged even if the storage is modified.

terms.tip: Three values that identify the session. Even if the server restarts, you can continue the same conversation by loading a session with the same values.
This is a transcript of the session's conversation. User messages, agent responses, tool calls, and results are stacked chronologically.
Temporary key-value data used only for this conversation. Leave values ​​such as progress steps or intermediate results. This is not a complete transcript of the conversation.
This service is responsible for creating, viewing, and adding and deleting events. Storage location and persistence vary depending on the implementation.

screens.outro: Now that we know the session configuration, let's check with the code what range the state is divided into.

screens.title: Range determined by State and prefix
screens.lead: Read the code below to see what range the prefix of the key name creates. The explanation on the right also describes symptoms when the range is set incorrectly.

data.code:
def update_state(callback_context):
    state = callback_context.state

    #Progression steps used only in the current session
    state["booking_step"] = "payment"

    #Preferences shared across all sessions of the same user
    state["user:language"] = "ko"

    #Settings shared across apps
    state["app:max_items"] = 20

    #Median value valid only during this call
    state["temp:draft_total"] = 31500

    return None

notes.note: When you change the value through the state of the callback context, the change is reflected in the event history. Avoid modifying the session object directly as it may not be reflected.

Keys without a prefix are currently session scoped. It is suitable for values ​​that are meaningful only to one conversation, such as progressing a conversation. When you save user preferences this way, they disappear from new sessions.
The user: prefix is shared across all sessions of the same user. Leave your preferences here. Placing a progress step here allows the user to start a new conversation with the previous step.
The app: prefix is shared across apps. Use only settings that must have the same value for all users. If you enter user-specific values, it will leak to other users.
The temp: prefix is a temporary value that is only valid for one invocation. It is used to pass values ​​between steps within the call and is not stored.

data.caption: Session Model Comparison
rows: Session: Container that holds id, events, and state
session: Loads the record before execution, prepends it to the input, and stores new items after execution.
Continue previous conversation with session identifier
Backends such as SQLite, Redis, SQLAlchemy, and OpenAI Conversations
Retrieve previous conversation based on session identifier
InMemory disappears, Database and VertexAi remain
If you use the same session id and the same storage backend, interrupted execution can be continued.
Continue with the same session identifier
Using session and continuing server management such as previous_response_id cannot be used together in one run.
The concept is the same, but the storage location varies depending on the environment in which you use it.
data.notes: OpenAI's Session API explains that a session maintains its configuration, conversations, and saved actions, and sending a message to an idle session starts a new turn. All three companies have the same concept of retrieving old conversations with identifiers. Although the name and storage are different, the structure of attaching an identifier to the conversation and recording it externally is the same.

screens.outro: Now that we've established the common structure of a session, let's look at the differences depending on who is responsible for recording it.

screens.title: When is state managed by the app and when is it managed by the platform?
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the differences depending on who is in charge of recording the conversation.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing the structure in which the app stores records and the structure in which the platform stores records, up and down.
labels: It must be possible to load it with the same ID

states.label: Managed by the app
states.body: I decide how to merge repositories and records. In the OpenAI Agents SDK, you can use an SDK session and use session_input_callback to control how to combine saved records with new input. The advantage is greater control and portability. You can move them to another repository or inspect and process the records yourself. Instead, storage operation and disaster recovery are also my responsibility.

states.label: The platform manages
states.body: The server holds the conversation or response chain, and the app carries only the identifier. It is lightweight as there is no need to operate a repository. Instead, there are restrictions on where and how it is stored. Mixing app management and platform management in one implementation creates ambiguity as to which has the history, so they cannot be used together. Either way, you should be able to load it with the same id even if the server is restarted.

screens.outro: Now that we have summarized the differences by type, let’s solve specific cases step by step.

screens.title: Explanatory example: When the status key range is incorrectly set
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The team creating the reservation service has stored the current booking step in a key called app:booking_step. During development, we only had one user, so we didn't see any issues.

steps.title: Step 1: User A proceeds to payment
steps.body: When user A proceeds with the conversation and moves on to the payment step, the booking_step value changes to payment. The key is app-scoped, so this value is shared across apps.

steps.title: Step 2: User B's new conversation is out of sync
steps.body: Immediately after that, when User B starts a new conversation, it has already started with the payment step, and they get an odd prompt. Another user's progress has been leaked. The key name is correct, but the range is wrong.

steps.title: Step 3: There is also the opposite mistake
steps.body: If you save the user's language preference without a prefix, it will work fine in the current session, but will be lost in new sessions. Users must restate their preferences each time. In this case, the user: scope is correct.

steps.title: Why is it discovered late?
steps.body: This error does not appear when there is only one user. Since multiple users have to start writing at the same time to mix the values, it passes in the verification environment but intermittently crashes in operation. Since the model seems to respond strangely to symptoms, we look for the cause in the model. In this case, check the event records and state values ​​together to check which keys are stored in which range.

steps.title: improvement
steps.body: Conversation progress is stored without prefix, user preferences are stored as user:, global settings are stored as app:, and intermediate values of a call are stored as temp:. We also establish naming rules to avoid repeatedly using keys with the same name, just with different ranges. Whenever we choose a key, we first ask who this value should be shared with and for how long. In the above example, replacing booking_step with a key without prefix solves the problem.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the scope issue, let's take a step-by-step look at restart recovery.

screens.title: Explained Case: From InMemory to Restart Recovery
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how your session management changes as you move from development to production.

stops.body: InMemorySessionService is suitable for prototyping. It requires no setup and is fast, but when you restart, both your session and state are lost. This seems fine during development, but when I use the same configuration in production, all conversations are lost on every restart.

In operation, replace it with a permanently stored service such as DatabaseSessionService or VertexAiSessionService. Since the agent code handles sessions through SessionService, persistence can be achieved simply by changing the service implementation.

After restarting, a session is loaded with the same app_name, user_id, and session id and the event continues. At this time, it is important to note that we do not create a new session object, but rather load an existing one. Users can continue saying “Please continue with what I said earlier” without realizing that the conversation has been interrupted.

Switching to permanent service doesn't end it. You should decide how your agent will behave when a session fails to load, in case the store slows down or hangs for a while. If you quietly start a new session, users won't know their history is gone. It is safer to let them know that the load failed and have them try again. Also, as events continue to accumulate, the records to be loaded become longer, so determine the period and length of storage.

In the OpenAI Agents SDK, you can continue interrupted execution by using the same session id and the same storage backend. Also, the state should contain only serializable values. Instead of putting complex objects in their entirety, leave only the identifier (e.g. order number instead of order object), and recreate or load the actual object when needed.

items.prompt: A session is a container that contains the ID, event, and state of a conversation.
items.answer: id, app_name, and user_id identify the conversation, events contain chronological history, and state contains temporary values used only for this conversation. Note that state is not the entire conversation history.

items.prompt: The scope of the state is determined by a prefix and its persistence depends on the session service.
items.answer: No prefix refers to the current session, user: refers to all sessions of the same user, app: refers to the entire app, and temp: refers to a single call. How long the value remains depends on which service you use: InMemory, Database, or VertexAi.

items.prompt: If the state is managed by the app, there is a lot of control; if the state is managed by the platform, it is light.
items.answer: App management allows greater control and portability as you can decide the storage and merging method, but it also comes with an operational burden. Platform management is lightweight as it only carries identifiers, but has limitations in how it is stored.

items.prompt: Restore to the same session ID as the persistent storage service in case of restart.
items.answer: In operation, a session service that is permanently stored is used, and the conversation continues even after restarting when the session is loaded with the same identifier. This is the same concept for all three: ADK, OpenAI, and Claude.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's think about it in relation to our own work.

screens.title: Connect to my work
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read the questions and think for yourself. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Key terms in this class are ADK Session, State scope, events, and OpenAI sessions. First, think about where the agent you create or write logs the conversation. Depending on whether it's process memory, a database, or the platform keeps it, what it looks like when the server restarts is completely different.

Whenever you add a state value, it's helpful to check three things: Who reads this value, how long should it remain, and to what extent should it be shared? The answers to these three questions lead to your prefix and repository selection.

Also, when developing, it is a good idea to create an inspection scenario that intentionally restarts the server. The most reliable check is to see if conversations continue with the same identifier after a restart. The quality of your session design is revealed not during normal times, but when obstacles arise.

Lastly, decide at this point whether it will be managed by the app or the platform. Consider app management if you need control and portability, or platform management if reducing operational burden is a priority, but keep in mind that you don't mix the two approaches in one implementation. Documenting the rationale for your choice makes it easier to judge when you change repositories later.

callout.label: Questions to Think About
callout.text: At what point does my work get stuck regarding ADK Session? Think about what information will be lost first when the server restarts, and what your users will have to do again if that information disappears.

checks.q: Match the following state prefixes with their scopes:
right: It is a temporary value that is only valid for one call.
Only used within the current session
Shared across all sessions of the same user
checks.explain: The range is determined by the prefix. Prefixless is appropriate for conversation progress, user: for user preference, app: for global settings, and temp: for the median value of one call.
checks.intro: Each state prefix has a different scope. Match prefixes with ranges.
checks.correctFeedback: All are correct. You correctly distinguished that no prefix, user:, app:, and temp: widens or narrows the scope to session, user, app, and one call, respectively.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Remember that the prefix determines the scope. The value shared on a per-user basis is user:, the app as a whole is app:, and the intermediate value used only in one call is temp:.

checks.q: Which statement correctly explains the difference between app management and platform management?
options: For app management, the server stores conversations and the app only carries the identifier.
Platform management is the responsibility of the developer, including storage operation and recovery from failures.
App management has a lot of control and portability, but storage management is also my responsibility, and platform management is light, but has limitations in storage methods.
Both methods cannot be loaded with the same ID when the server is restarted.
checks.explain: App management involves operational burden instead of deciding how to merge with the repository. Platform management is light, but there are restrictions on storage location and storage method.

wrong.0: That's the explanation of platform management.
wrong.1: That's the explanation of app management.
wrong.3: Either way, you should be able to load it with the same ID after restarting.

checks.intro: The benefits and burdens vary depending on who manages the session. Pick out the differences between the two methods.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. App management involves storage management instead of gaining control, and platform management is lightweight but has limitations in storage methods.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is an example where the responsibility for the two approaches is reversed. Compare again based on the fact that app management is directly responsible for storage operation and disaster recovery.

checks.q: When the server restarts while the order is in progress, the agent does not know the previous conversation. What recovery method is appropriate for my production environment?
options: Keep the InMemorySessionService and ask the user to repeat it from the beginning
If you put an entire complex object in the state, it will remain even if you restart.
Change the state by directly modifying the session object
Change to a permanently stored session service and load it with the same app_name, user_id, and session id.
checks.explain: When InMemory is restarted, the session and state disappear. Use a service that is permanently stored, such as a Database or VertexAi service, and load a session with the same identifier to continue the event.

wrong.0: InMemory is for prototype use, so recovery after restart is impossible.
wrong.1: Only serializable values should be left in the state, and complex objects should only have identifiers.
wrong.2: Changing the session object directly will not be reflected in the event record and should be avoided.

checks.intro: This is an operational example where the conversation disappeared after restarting the server. Choose the recovery method that suits you.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. You can continue previous events by using a session service that is permanently stored and loading it with the same app_name, user_id, and session id.
checks.incorrectFeedback: When InMemorySessionService is restarted, the session and state are lost. The key is to reload the session with three identifiers, such as persistent storage.

glossary.def: An object that contains one conversation thread between a user and an agent. It has id, event record, and state.
The effective range is determined by the prefix. No prefix is ​​a session, user: is a user, app: is an app, temp: is a single call.
A chronological record of user messages, responses, and tool actions within a session.
The SDK's session memory stores conversation history and automatically merges it with the input of the next execution.
It is a function called during execution and is a passage to safely change the state through the state of the context.

misconceptions.myth: state is the entire conversation history.
misconceptions.fact: Conversation records are events, and state is temporary key-value data used during a conversation.

misconceptions.myth: The state remains even if the server is restarted.
misconceptions.fact: It disappears from the InMemory service. If you want to maintain it after restart, you must use a persistent service such as Database or VertexAi.

misconceptions.myth: The state key only needs to have the correct name.
misconceptions.fact: The scope varies depending on the prefix. If written incorrectly, the value may be leaked to other users or lost in a new session.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: A session is a container that holds the ID, event, and state of a conversation.
The scope of the state is determined by the prefix and its persistence depends on the session service.
If the app manages the state, there is a lot of control; if the platform manages the state, it is light.
To prepare for restarts, use a persistent storage service and restore with the same session ID.
